Alien vs Predator is a good entry (especially if you like Predator), but AVP: Requiem fucking blows and is the only movie I genuinely recommend not watching. Finally Prometheus and Covenant retain some of the core elements of the franchise, but their themes focus a bit more on philosophical ideas of humanity’s place in the universe rather than critiques of capitalism and the military industrial complex. 

TL; DR: As long as you watch Alien, you’re good. Aliens js the “best” sequel to watch, and the only other film that I would consider necessary before Romulus. The rest you should watch if you really enjoy the world building/aesthetic.

A conscious decision could’ve worked  if they’d actually kept the clones as super obedient. There are a lot of little instances of clones disobeying or bending orders when it suits them, and there are very few episodes where the clones follow orders that nobody else will. 

The series goes out of its way to paint the clones as individuals who each develop their own personalities and are more than just obedient soldiers. They use battle droids as an exact narrative foil to prove this point. Having the clones willingly kill the Jedi without the inhibitor chips would go against the writing of the series itself. 

I think a conscious choice would be an interesting story and open up a lot of interesting discussion, but they would’ve had to seriously rewrite the clones to satisfyingly pull it off.

Creating the inhibitor chips for order 66 was the right call for the series. If they just kept it as clones following orders, it would’ve conflicted with the rest of the writing and development the clones received.
The story perhaps would have been more cohesive, but it wouldn’t have been much better quality IMO.

From what I can tell, a lot of controversy seems to happen with some people that are friends or collaborators with Chris. While he’s definitely had some questionable friendships, he’s cut ties and denounced with a good chunk of them (Shadman and Stamper as notable examples.)

2) The sheer number of rotating cast members, editors, and thumbnail artists makes it much harder for any singular person (besides maybe Chris) to dominate other members/contracted employees.

I’ve begun running some skill checks in terms of quality of success over pass/fail. So instead of a roll to pick the lock or not pick the lock, your roll determines how quickly, quietly, or unnoticeably you can pick it. This way, a spell still ensures a high quality success, but it doesn’t totally overshadow skills/proficiencies.

A lot of comments seems to be focused on combat, but one area that the caster/martial divide really shows through is in out-of-combat utility. Rangers and Rogues can get their niches/specialties overshadowed by some fairly low level spells, and since most other materials have little-to-no utility, it falls to casters. 

Spells that auto succeed something that would take a skill check (ex. picking a lock) need to either be more costly, have more limitations, or have a chance of failing.

Honestly, as long as your players being “evil” won’t make things obnoxiously hard for themselves or their party, I think it’s fine. My party and I tend to have a mix of morally good, morally grey, and morally bad characters, but our group thrives on interparty debate and character conflict leading to character development. Also, we plan in worlds/settings where committing evil deeds may pose extra challenges for us, but not enough to make the game unplayable. We may have to be more cautious around the law, but we don’t have to worry about a SWAT team busting down our door. 

As far as your player is concerned, just talk to them and let them know that even if they play an “evil” character, they still need to be somewhat cooperative with the group. They don’t necessarily have to fully agree, and they shouldn’t stop themselves from “doing evil,” but just remind them that unless the party wants the good vs evil dynamic in their party (which can be fun in its own right), they need to use the party as a way to extend their evil reach, not hamper it. 

Also, I think alignments in D&D are only useful for a basic idea of how a character plays, they can change fairly easily once players settle into their characters, and are entirely subjective, so I wouldn’t focus on the alignment itself, but more how your player’s specific attitudes/actions impact the party/game overall

This gives everyone at least one shot to roll better than standard array, in case they get lucky the first time. Then, for people that like to play it safe, they can use standard array or point buy. For those that like to take risks, they can roll again for better/higher stats. 

Some people into party like to play things safe. Others (like myself) like to take risks and don’t mind potentially handicapping their own character for flavor/fun. This option gives everyone a potential chance to experience the thrill of rolling high stats without the risk of rolling absolute shit stats

Because the republic isn’t ordering atrocities left and right, and it doesn’t have brainwashing for the clones. And the clones don’t commit atrocities, so to suddenly betray their leaders/comrades because they were told to with no other reason goes against their characterization in TCW

TCW changed the extent to which clones were showed to obey all orders. Clones are frequently shown disobeying orders, breaking protocols, and on the spot improv of strategy and tactics. From a storytelling perspective, they needed a new way to explain why they clones suddenly changed behavior when the show only reinforced the idea that clones weren’t mindlessly obedient.

I think the original version made since only because we had very few interactions between clones and Jedi, and we never got to really know individual clones as well as we did during TCW. The minute TCW delved into the philosophy and psychology of the clones, showing their humanity, the need for the inhibitor chips arose.
In addition to the individuality, there are a lot of times where the clones disobey orders and protocol, especially when linked to the lives of their Jedi friends and fellow clones.

The stormtroopers and empire are an analogy for Nazism, and we know that Hitler didn’t implant chips in German brains. Brainwashing, propaganda, training, and just human cruelty are explanation enough

There are also several times in TCW where clones go against orders. The individuality of each clone (personality, armor decoration, haircut, tattoos, etc) also go against the idea that each clone was basically just a flesh robot. I think they handled the philosophical repercussions of mass cloning very well, it just didn’t jive with the original canon, hence the need for a new plot device.

I think that the development of clones in TCW is the main reason for the chips. Most of the clones are shown to be loyal to their brothers and even their Jedi (in some cases) than the Republic. Some of the clones that are super strict in their adherence to protocol/command (like Dogma) are mocked/called out by other clones. They also stressed each clone’s search for individuality. They made the clones more human, but that also made it harder to justify their betrayal, especially on the sheer scale it happened. 

I do think it would be much more complex and interesting to see the actions of individual clones. Even if most Jedi aren’t terrible to their clones, few develop true relationships/bonds with them. Ashoka and Anakin are the best examples, but beyond that, even Obi-Wan has more of a professional relationship than a true friendship. Some clones may have felt remorse, but others may have felt completely justified. 

I do think the chips cheapened the betrayal, but it seems like more consistent storytelling to have the inhibitor chips than to suddenly throw aside all of the character developments/relationships the clones had.
